newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major staring electoral defeat in face.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major staring electoral defeat in face.

text.p: John Major, one of the most unlikely of British prime ministers, faces electoral humiliation on Thursday after 4-1/2 years spent skirmishing with right-wing guerrillas in his own party and a rejuvenated Labour Party.
Major won the 1992 election against the odds and almost single-handedly. He has tried valiantly to pull off the same trick again but the polls show he will almost certainly fail.

Since taking over from Margaret Thatcher in 1990, Major has been blamed for weak leadership, lack of direction and a number of policy disasters which sent his personal rating, and that of his ruling Conservatives, to all-time lows in the polls.

But Major was probably the only man capable of keeping his party together as it tore itself apart over Europe and for many voters the "grey man" of British politics is the only good reason to vote Conservative in this election.

His party's six-week campaign was based on Major, the government's economic policy and his personal qualities. Here is a man you can trust, a man with experience, a man who can fight Britain's corner in Europe, the Conservatives told voters.
Memories of his government's perceived ineptitude faded during the longest campaign in 80 years, but Major was unable to mask the Conservatives' deep splits over Britain's links with Europe.

On April 16, in the most electrifying moment of the campaign, Major appealed over the heads of 44 million voters to his Eurosceptic members of parliament who are demanding that Britain never enters a single currency.

"Like me or loathe me, do not bind my hands when I am negotiating on behalf of the British nation," he said in an impassioned defence of his "wait and see" policy. To add to Major's problems, the working class boy who took over a party traditionally run by the rich and titled has been eclipsed by Tony Blair, the privately educated socialist who revamped the Labour Party's "spit and sawdust" image.

Major has mocked Blair's leadership qualities and belittled his lack of experience. The Conservatives even launched an advertisement depicting Blair as a ventriloquist's dummy on the lap of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

But Blair, who will become Britain's youngest prime minister this century if he wins, and his restructuring of Labour have captured the imagination of a public which polls suggest is increasingly fed up with 18 years of Conservative rule.
This election is the toughest battle of Major's political career but the inner steel of the grey-haired, grey-suited man often mocked by comedians for being dull has clinched victory for him before.

When the Conservatives dumped the increasingly autocratic Thatcher in November 1990, Major emerged from the pack as a compromise candidate, the calm after the storm. Taking to his much-mocked soap box to appeal directly to voters, he defied political pundits to land the April 1992 general election.
After telling his right-wing opponents to "put up or shut up," he won a June 1995 leadership contest in a mutinous Conservative party split over Britain's role in Europe.
After considering the alternative candidate -- right-winger John Redwood -- party members decided Major was the only man who could win the next election.
Whatever Major's faults may be, he is a great survivor.

He overcame the ignominy of sterling's withdrawal from the European currency grid in 1992 and was mercilessly mocked for a "Back to Basics" morality campaign that backfired amid a flurry of sex scandals and sleaze allegations in his party.
He fought hard to bring peace to Northern Ireland, one of the 20th century's most insoluble guerrilla conflicts.
He reacted with icy calm when Irish Republican Army guerrillas mortar bombed his Downing Street residence. His quiet authority during the Gulf War sent his popularity soaring.
His diffidence proved effective. "Don't forget I am an Englishman. The English tend to be understated," he once said.
But his turbulent years in power tend to be remembered more for the lows than the highs -- party mutinies, resignations sparked by scandals, embarrassing policy U-turns.
Major's darkest hour came in September 1992 when speculators forced the pound out of the European Union's semi-fixed exchange rate mechanism.
No minister resigned for this humiliation and the public did not forgive Major, who has since admitted the experience left deep scars.

Major, born in London on March 29, 1943, saw poverty as a child. His father, originally a trapeze artist in a vaudeveille act, had a factory making garden gnome ornaments that went bust, forcing him to swop their family home for a modest apartment.
He left school at 16 and did several different jobs before going into banking. He worked in Hong Kong and Nigeria, where he suffered a serious leg injury in a car crash.
He entered parliament in 1979 as member for Huntingdon, north of London, after Conservative talent scouts spotted him working in local politics.

Major rose to become Minister of Social Security and in 1987 Chief Secretary (junior minister) to the Treasury before being catapulted into the spotlight when Thatcher unexpectedly made him Foreign Secretary in July 1989.
Three months later, he became Chancellor of the Exchequer, articulating Thatcher's anti-inflation policy.
Major's greatest passion is sport. He loves to attend Chelsea soccer club games and has the results of cricket internationals relayed to his plane on foreign trips.
Major's wife Norma, whom he married in 1970, is a fervent opera fan. In 1987, she published a biography of Australian soprano Joan Sutherland. The Majors have two children, Elizabeth and James.
